# Selection — TRD §15 row 9: chain-head discovery for a brand-new device

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 9 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.5, §13.6, §13.8, §7.3, §7.5 · PRD §7.6 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/head-discovery.json`](../../test/vectors/head-discovery.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-head-discovery-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-head-discovery-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) is why this row became load-bearing;
[row 11](./row-11-enrollment-ceremony.md) discharges two thirds of it and gained a bound field doing so;
[row 4](./row-4-envelope-format.md) frames the request.
**Amends:** [row 11](./row-11-enrollment-ceremony.md)'s transcript, which now binds the epoch head.

---

## The selection

```
Three arrival paths, and only one is genuinely brand-new.

  1. Enrollment through an existing device       (§13.6, row 11)
     The head arrives THROUGH THE PERSON. Row 11's transcript now binds the
     epoch head, so the five typed symbols authenticate where the lineage is
     as well as whose key it is. No trust in the service at all.

  2. Migration or fidelity-archive restore       (row 10, §9.3, §14)
     The package is user-held and carries a signed head. Same in kind as 1:
     the anchor came from outside the service.

  3. Recovery with no surviving device           (§13.8)
     The only genuinely brand-new case. It asks, and this is the asking.

The head assertion

  Assertion = Ed25519( K_auth ;
                LP("done/head-assert/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(dec epoch)
                || LP(hex epoch_head) || LP(hex client_nonce)
                || LP(dec issued_at) )

  client_nonce  32 fresh bytes from the arriving device, per request.
  issued_at     seconds. Displayed to the person; never enforced.
  K_auth        the authorization signing key (§13.5). Not row 5's K_accept.

The rules

  1. Refuse an assertion answering a nonce this device did not send.
  2. Record the head at first contact. From then on §13.5's ancestor rule
     applies and this row is finished.
  3. On path 3, show the epoch, its age, and the device list it implies —
     because that display is the only remaining check.

The residual, stated

  A hostile authorization service can serve a recovering device a stale,
  self-consistent head at first contact. It CANNOT also show current
  content: revocation is atomic with rotation (§7.5), so a hidden
  revocation is a hidden generation, and a device on the stale generation
  cannot read anything written after it. The attack degrades to a
  partition, which is availability rather than integrity.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. Why this row stopped being optional

§13.5 states the problem and declines to solve it, in a sentence that is easy to read as closure:

> A returning client remembers the newest head it has seen and rejects an ancestor. A **brand-new** client
> trusts the service to identify the current head; there is no mechanism that fixes that.

That was tolerable while nothing depended on it. **[Row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) is what changed that**: the
whole accepted-chain guarantee is stated relative to a head the client believes is current, so "no mechanism
fixes that" is now the foundation of the finalization boundary rather than a footnote about a fresh install.

**This row does not fix it either, and says so.** What it does is narrow what _brand-new_ covers, then bound
what is left. Those are different acts from solving it, and conflating them is the failure mode here — a
construction that looks like a fix and is a trust-on-first-use with extra signatures.

---

## 2. Two of the three arrival paths are not brand-new, and one of them was already in the tree

The premise worth interrogating is _brand-new_. A device with no history still arrives somehow, and how it
arrives determines what it can be told by whom.

**Enrollment is not brand-new, because there is another device in the room.** §13.6's whole second gate is a
person mediating between an existing device and a new one, and the existing device knows exactly where the
lineage is. [Row 11](./row-11-enrollment-ceremony.md) was already carrying a transcript through that channel and
already binding the epoch **number**; binding the epoch **head** costs two bytes on each side and makes the same
five typed symbols authenticate the lineage's position as well as the wrapping key.

**So row 11 is amended, one commit after being selected.** Its transcript gains `epoch_head`, its vectors gain a
`stale-epoch-head` negative, and its short string changes. That is the dependency order doing its job rather
than a defect: row 9 is downstream of row 11 in the register and upstream of it in fact, and nothing has been
built, so the amendment costs a regenerated vector file. **After the first deployment it would have cost a
protocol version.**

**Migration and archive restore are not brand-new either**, for the same structural reason: the package is
user-held, so the anchor came from outside the service. Row 10 owns its format and inherits the requirement that
a signed head travel in it.

**What is left is recovery with no surviving device** — §13.8's case where the code and the ciphertext are all
that remain. That is one path, it is rare, it is deliberate, and it is already a screen the person is reading
carefully. Those four properties are what make the residual below acceptable rather than merely unavoidable.

---

## 3. The nonce, and what it actually separates

The assertion binds a nonce the arriving device generated. That does not stop a service that holds `K_auth` from
signing whatever it likes — nothing does — and the value is not in pretending otherwise.

**What it separates is a hostile relay from a hostile authorization service**, which is the distinction §7.3
draws and §7.5 leans on throughout. Without the nonce, a head assertion is a standing artifact: signed once,
valid forever, re-servable by anything in the path. Any relay, cache or intermediary could hold last month's
assertion and hand it to a device arriving today, and **the attack would need no key at all.** With the nonce,
replay requires `K_auth`, which moves the residual from _anyone in the path_ to _the authorization service
itself_.

**That is the same move §7.5 makes and it is worth naming as a pattern**, because it is the one this design
keeps reaching for: not eliminating a trusted party, but reducing the set of parties who have to be trusted
until only the one you already named remains.

**`issued_at` is bound and not enforced.** A device recovering after total loss has no trustworthy clock, so a
freshness _check_ would be theatre. It is signed because it is _displayed_, and rule 3 makes that display part
of the construction — a person who sees "this workspace as of six weeks ago" while recovering a workspace they
used yesterday has been given the check the cryptography cannot make.

---

## 4. The residual, and the bound that makes it survivable

**The attack.** A hostile authorization service serves a recovering device epoch _n_ rather than the current
_n+1_, where _n+1_ committed the revocation of a credential the attacker holds. The device records epoch _n_ at
first contact, §13.5's ancestor rule locks it there, and the revoked credential's writes verify.

**The bound, and it falls out of §7.5 rather than being added here.** Revocation is not an epoch change; it is
**one atomic security boundary** — the authorization successor, _a client-produced content-key generation with
its reader and recovery wraps_, and the finalization boundary, committed together. So:

> **A hidden revocation is a hidden rotation.** Serving epoch _n_ means serving generation _g_, and everything
> the honest devices have written since the rotation is sealed under _g+1_. The attacker cannot supply it — that
> is what excluding the credential meant — so the device sees a workspace frozen at the moment of the rotation,
> plus whatever the revoked credential writes under the old key.

**The attack therefore cannot present a stale authorization state and current content at the same time.** It
degrades to a partition, which is availability rather than integrity, and which §7.5 already records as a
failure the threat model permits. And the symptom — _everything after some date is missing_ — is the one thing a
person running a recovery is guaranteed to be looking at.

**What this does not cover, said plainly.** A workspace whose history is genuinely quiet since the rotation
presents almost identically either way, and a person recovering an abandoned workspace has little to compare
against. The bound is real and it is not a guarantee; it converts a silent integrity failure into a loud
availability one, in the common case.

---

## 5. Three narrowings considered and declined

**A second independent source for the first head.** Ask the relay and the durable store and require agreement.
Declined because they are not independent: §16 has one operator behind both, and §11.3 test 9 exists precisely
because the whole provider account is a single failure domain. Two answers from one party is one answer.

**A user-held anchor the person compares.** A short workspace fingerprint shown at recovery. Declined on
[row 11](./row-11-enrollment-ceremony.md)'s own reasoning — a comparison is satisfied by pressing the
affirmative button — and worse here, because on path 3 the person has nothing to compare _against_. Row 11 could
demand a transcription because there were two screens; this path has one.

**Binding the head into the recovery envelope.** Declined as impossible rather than unwise: the envelope is
sealed once at account creation (§13.8) and the head advances afterwards. Naming it because it is the first
thing that suggests itself, and the reason it fails is the reason no static user-held secret can carry
freshness.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost        | Size                                                                         |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per arrival | One round trip, one Ed25519 signature, one verify. **Once per device, ever** |
| Bundle      | **Nothing.** Ed25519 and SHA-256 are WebCrypto (row 1)                       |
| Row 11      | Two bound bytes and a regenerated vector file                                |
| The person  | One screen at recovery, which §13.8 already puts in front of them            |

**The service gains a signing operation it cannot batch**, since the nonce is per request — but it is per device
arrival rather than per envelope, so it is not row 5's hot path and `K_auth` does not become a hot key. **That
was the reason to keep `K_auth` distinct from `K_accept`** and it now has a second justification: the key that
signs epochs signs this too, at the same rate epochs change, and row 5's acceptance key stays the only one on
the delivery path.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**The recovery screen is part of the construction, not decoration around it.** Rule 3 makes the display of
epoch, age and implied device list the last check on path 3, so it is an obligation with a security purpose and
not copy. It should say what it is asking the person to notice, which is the hard part and is a question for
review 3b rather than an answer from here.

**One obligation that is easy to lose.** _Record the head at first contact_ has to be durable and atomic with
whatever else recovery writes; a device that verifies a head and then fails to persist it before its next launch
gets a second first contact, and the exposure this row bounds to one moment becomes a repeated one. That is the
same class of requirement as §13.6's crash-safe promotion, and it should be tested the same way.

**Not in this row.** How an epoch head is computed is §13.5's and **row 7**'s; this row consumes it as an opaque
digest, which is all it is entitled to assume. How the request is framed is **row 4**'s. What a migration
package carries is **row 10**'s, and the requirement that it carry a signed head is stated here and owed there.

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-head-discovery-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and
`pnpm check` now runs it with the other eight.

**Three assertions and nine negatives.** The current head answering the nonce that was sent; the same head for a
second device, which is what makes the first one unreplayable; and a genuine assertion for the previous epoch,
correctly signed and correctly nonced, refused only by the ancestor rule and only by a device that already has a
head.

**The coverage audit refused the first pass, on the one field this row exists for.** The obvious replay
negative — offer a device an assertion answering somebody else's nonce — fails on a string comparison between
the nonce the device sent and the nonce the assertion carries. **That comparison fails whether or not the nonce
is signed at all**, so it was testing the client rule and nothing about the binding, and eliding `client_nonce`
from the message left it still failing.

The isolating negative is the same replay with the carried nonce **rewritten** to match, so the device's own
comparison passes and only the signature can refuse it — which is also the actual attack, since a nonce that
were carried but unsigned could simply be overwritten in transit. **A construction whose most important field
was tested by a string comparison is exactly the shape the audit was built to catch**, and it caught it here
three rows after it was built.
